## Why this matters {#sec-ds-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Until now the array was the *input*: we read it to answer one question. In this chapter the array is the *product*. A caller keeps sending operations (insert, delete, take a snapshot, ask for a random element, clear everything) and each one must stay cheap, usually $O(1)$. Every structure here is an ordinary array plus one extra index or one counter, and the design work is choosing that index and keeping it correct.
:::

The chapter builds directly on earlier ones. From @sec-arr it takes the packed array and the amortised doubling of @sec-arr-vec, which every structure here relies on when it appends. From @sec-hash it takes the hash map, with its expected $O(1)$ cost and its weakness against adversarial keys (@sec-hash-sets, @sec-hash-anti); here we open the box and build the table ourselves. From @sec-bst it takes the floor search (`bisect_right(a, x) - 1`) that answers a snapshot query. @sec-idx taught that an array can be indexed by its own values, which is exactly direct addressing, and @sec-mat used the same "one more index" thinking for two dimensions.

These designs come up constantly in interviews ("design a set with random access", "design a snapshot array", "design an LFU cache") and in contests as the hidden step that turns $O(nq)$ into $O(n + q)$: an "assign all" query, a "reset between test cases", a "flip every bit". They share three habits:

- **Keep the array packed.** If no caller reads the order, a deletion can move the last element into the hole instead of shifting everything.
- **Index by what the query asks for.** A query about frequencies is answered by a container indexed by frequency; a query about versions by records tagged with versions.
- **Never do work you can defer.** A snapshot is a counter bump, a reset is a clock tick, a global flip is a flag; the cost reappears later as one comparison per touched cell.

The lessons A1–A5 teach one tool each, and the patterns P1–P5 put each tool to work on solved problems. The next chapter, @sec-cnt, turns from designing structures to counting over all subarrays, pairs and triples.

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. Swap-with-last deletion {#sec-ds-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Removing an element from the middle of a list normally shifts every later element one step left: $O(n)$ work (`list.pop(i)` or `vector::erase`, the cost @sec-arr-vec warns about). But if the container has *no order to preserve*, as in a set, a multiset or a pool of live objects, you can delete with one move: copy the **last** element into the doomed slot, then shrink the array by one. The array stays packed into $[0, n)$, so `len(a)` is still the size and `a[randrange(n)]` is still a uniformly random element. The only catch is bookkeeping: the element that moved now sits at a different index, so anything that records positions must be updated for it too.
:::

The invariant, in one line: **after every operation the live elements occupy exactly `a[0..n-1]`, and `pos[v]` is the slot of every live `v`.** Swap-with-last preserves it because it changes only slot `i` (now holding the old tail) and slot `n-1` (dropped), and it repairs `pos` for the one element that moved.

```{python}
def swap_remove(a, pos, v):
    """Delete value v from a packed list in O(1), keeping pos (value -> index) correct.
    The order of `a` is irrelevant (it is a set), so v's slot is overwritten with the tail."""
    i = pos[v]                             # slot holding v
    last = a[-1]
    a[i] = last                            # the tail fills the hole
    pos[last] = i                          # ... and its recorded index follows it
    del pos[v]                             # drop v AFTER, so that v == last still works
    a.pop()                                # shrink the (now duplicated) tail
    return i


a = [10, 20, 30, 40]
pos = {10: 0, 20: 1, 30: 2, 40: 3}
swap_remove(a, pos, 20)
assert a == [10, 40, 30] and pos == {10: 0, 30: 2, 40: 1}
swap_remove(a, pos, 30)                    # removing the tail itself: i == n-1
assert a == [10, 40] and pos == {10: 0, 40: 1}
for _ in range(300):
    b = random.sample(range(1000), random.randint(1, 8))
    q = {x: k for k, x in enumerate(b)}
    v = random.choice(b)
    swap_remove(b, q, v)
    assert set(b) == set(q) and v not in q and all(q[x] == k for k, x in enumerate(b))
```

Swap-with-last on `a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]`, removing `20, 60, 10, 30`. Each removal is one copy, one `pos` repair and one pop; nothing after the hole shifts. The final state is `a = [40, 50]` with `pos = {40: 0, 50: 1}`.

:::

**What swap-with-last costs you.** The order of the array is destroyed. That is free for a set, but it rules the trick out whenever someone reads the order: a queue, a sorted array, a history. Two honest alternatives exist when order matters. A **tombstone** marks the slot dead instead of removing it ($O(1)$ delete, but the array now has holes, so sampling and `len` need extra counters), and a periodic **compaction** removes all tombstones in one $O(n)$ pass once, say, half the slots are dead, which keeps the amortised cost $O(1)$.

### The array underneath: growth and shrinking {#sec-ds-a1-grow}

Every structure in this chapter appends to a dynamic array, and @sec-arr-vec proved that doubling the capacity when it is full makes `append` $O(1)$ amortised. Structures that also delete a lot may want to give memory back by **shrinking**. The tempting rule "halve the capacity when the array is half full" is a trap: at the boundary, one `append` doubles (copying $n$ elements) and the next `pop` halves (copying $n$ again), so alternating the two costs $\Theta(n)$ per operation. The standard fix is hysteresis: **halve only when the array is a quarter full.** After any resize the array is exactly half full, so at least $n/4$ operations must happen before the next resize, and they pay for its $O(n)$ copy.

```{python}
def resize_copies(ops, shrink_at):
    """Elements copied by a dynamic array that doubles when full and halves its capacity
    when size <= cap * shrink_at. ops is a string of '+' (append) and '-' (pop)."""
    cap, size, copies = 1, 0, 0
    for op in ops:
        if op == "+":
            if size == cap:
                copies += size
                cap *= 2
            size += 1
        else:
            size -= 1
            if cap > 1 and size <= cap * shrink_at:
                copies += size
                cap //= 2
    return copies


fill = "+" * 1024                           # size 1024 = capacity: right at the boundary
thrash = fill + "+-" * 500
assert resize_copies(thrash, 1 / 2) > 500 * 1000      # every pair copies ~1024 elements twice
assert resize_copies(thrash, 1 / 4) < 3 * len(thrash) # quarter rule: O(1) amortised
for _ in range(200):                                  # and in general, on random sequences
    ops, size = [], 0
    for _ in range(random.randint(1, 400)):
        op = "+" if size == 0 or random.random() < 0.55 else "-"
        size += 1 if op == "+" else -1
        ops.append(op)
    assert resize_copies(ops, 1 / 4) <= 3 * len(ops)
```

## A2. Snapshots and versions {#sec-ds-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A snapshot "looks like" a full copy of the array, so the reflex is to store a copy on every `snap()`. But between two snapshots only the cells that were written change; a cell that is never written needs no history at all. So turn the representation inside out. Instead of *snapshot $\to$ whole array*, keep *cell $\to$ list of `(version, value)` records*. `snap()` is then just `version += 1`, `set(i, v)` records `(version, v)` on cell $i$ only, and `get(i, s)` asks cell $i$ for its newest record with version $\le s$. Versions on one cell only increase, so that lookup is the floor search of @sec-bst-a2: `bisect_right(versions, s) - 1`.
:::

**Two invariants.** (1) `snap()` copies nothing; it advances one integer, `version`, and returns the old value as the snapshot id. (2) Each cell's record list is sorted by version with no repeated version, and its last record is the cell's current value. A second write under the same version *overwrites* the last record, because a snapshot sees only the state at the moment it is taken, not the writes in between.

```{python}
class VersionedArray:
    """Snapshots in O(1): each cell keeps (version, value) records, written only on set."""

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.vers = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        self.vals = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        self.version = 0

    def set(self, i, v):
        if self.vers[i] and self.vers[i][-1] == self.version:
            self.vals[i][-1] = v               # same version: overwrite, don't append
        else:
            self.vers[i].append(self.version)
            self.vals[i].append(v)

    def snap(self):
        self.version += 1
        return self.version - 1                # the id the writes so far were tagged with

    def get(self, i, sid):
        p = bisect.bisect_right(self.vers[i], sid) - 1   # newest record with version <= sid
        return self.vals[i][p] if p >= 0 else 0          # never written by then: default 0


va = VersionedArray(3)
va.set(0, 5); va.set(2, 1)
assert va.snap() == 0
va.set(0, 6); va.set(0, 7)
assert va.snap() == 1
va.set(1, 4)
assert va.snap() == 2
va.set(0, 9)
assert va.vers[0] == [0, 1, 3] and va.vals[0] == [5, 7, 9]   # 6 was overwritten by 7
assert [va.get(0, s) for s in range(3)] == [5, 7, 7]
assert [va.get(1, s) for s in range(3)] == [0, 0, 4]
# stress against copying the whole array at every snapshot
for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 4)
    fast, cur, copies = VersionedArray(n), [0] * n, []
    for _ in range(30):
        if random.random() < 0.6:
            i, v = random.randrange(n), random.randint(1, 9)
            fast.set(i, v); cur[i] = v
        else:
            assert fast.snap() == len(copies)
            copies.append(cur[:])
    assert all(fast.get(i, s) == copies[s][i] for s in range(len(copies)) for i in range(n))
```

```cpp
// One snap is a counter bump; a set tags the CURRENT version.
struct VersionedArray {
    vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> col;   // per cell: (version, value), versions increasing
    int version = 0;
    VersionedArray(int n) : col(n) {}
    void set(int i, int v) {
        if (!col[i].empty() && col[i].back().first == version) col[i].back().second = v;
        else col[i].push_back(make_pair(version, v));
    }
    int snap() { return version++; }
    int get(int i, int sid) {            // newest record with version <= sid
        const vector<pair<int,int>>& c = col[i];
        int lo = 0, hi = (int)c.size();
        while (lo < hi) { int m = (lo + hi) / 2; if (c[m].first <= sid) lo = m + 1; else hi = m; }
        return lo ? c[lo - 1].second : 0;
    }
};
```

Per-cell version histories after `set(0,5) set(2,1) snap set(0,6) set(0,7) snap set(1,4) snap set(0,9)`. Three snapshots cost three counter bumps; only the five effective writes are stored (the write of $6$ was overwritten under the same version). Reading snapshot $1$ takes each cell's newest record with version $\le 1$ (amber): cell $0$ gives $7$, cell $2$ gives $1$, and cell $1$ has none, so it reads the default $0$.

### Undo by logging old values {#sec-ds-a2-rollback}

Sometimes the past is not *read*, it is *returned to*: "undo everything since the checkpoint". Then the cheapest history is a **change log**: before each write, push `(index, old value)` onto a stack. A checkpoint is the current length of the log, and rolling back pops entries and restores the old values, newest first. Each write is logged and undone at most once, so rollback is $O(1)$ amortised per write. This is how a disjoint-set union "with rollback" and many backtracking searches undo their changes.

```{python}
class RollbackArray:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.a = [0] * n
        self.log = []                      # stack of (index, old value)

    def set(self, i, v):
        self.log.append((i, self.a[i]))
        self.a[i] = v

    def checkpoint(self):
        return len(self.log)

    def rollback(self, cp):
        while len(self.log) > cp:
            i, old = self.log.pop()
            self.a[i] = old


ra = RollbackArray(3)
ra.set(0, 5)
cp = ra.checkpoint()
ra.set(0, 6); ra.set(2, 8)
ra.rollback(cp)
assert ra.a == [5, 0, 0] and ra.log == [(0, 0)]
for _ in range(200):                       # nested checkpoints against saved copies
    n = random.randint(1, 4)
    ra, saved = RollbackArray(n), []
    for _ in range(30):
        r = random.random()
        if r < 0.5:
            ra.set(random.randrange(n), random.randint(1, 9))
        elif r < 0.75:
            saved.append((ra.checkpoint(), ra.a[:]))
        elif saved:
            cp, copy = saved.pop()
            ra.rollback(cp)
            assert ra.a == copy
```

Versions and rollback answer different questions. A versioned array reads *any* old version at any time, at $O(\log k)$ per read; a rollback log returns to the most recent checkpoints only (last in, first out), but the current array is always a plain array with $O(1)$ reads. Full persistence, where an old version can itself be modified, needs persistent trees and belongs to the tree volume.

## A3. Counters of counters {#sec-ds-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Some questions are not about a value but about its **count**: "is some value present exactly 3 times?", "give me the most frequent element", "give me a key with the smallest count". A dictionary `value -> count` makes updates cheap but the query a scan. The fix is a **second container indexed by the count itself**. In its smallest form, `cnt[f]` says *how many* values have frequency $f$. In richer forms, `levels[f]` holds *which* values have it. Because one update changes one value's count by exactly one, it moves that value between two **adjacent** levels, and the extreme non-empty level can be tracked with a single integer.
:::

The smallest version, the **count of counts**:

```{python}
def count_of_counts(stream):
    """freq[x] = occurrences of x; cnt[f] = how many values occur exactly f times."""
    freq, cnt = Counter(), Counter()
    for x in stream:
        if freq[x]:
            cnt[freq[x]] -= 1                  # x leaves its old level ...
        freq[x] += 1
        cnt[freq[x]] += 1                      # ... and joins the next one
    return freq, cnt


cc_freq, cc_cnt = count_of_counts([4, 4, 2, 4, 2, 7])
assert cc_freq == Counter({4: 3, 2: 2, 7: 1})
assert {f: c for f, c in cc_cnt.items() if c} == {1: 1, 2: 1, 3: 1}
for _ in range(200):
    s = [random.randint(0, 5) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 20))]
    fr, ct = count_of_counts(s)
    assert all(ct[f] == sum(1 for c in fr.values() if c == f) for f in range(1, 21))
```

When the query must *return* an extreme value, the levels hold the values themselves. A value is pushed onto `levels[f]` at the moment its count *reaches* $f$, and an integer `top` remembers the highest non-empty level:

```
push(x):
    f = freq[x] + 1; freq[x] = f       # 1) update the plain counter
    levels[f].push(x)                  # 2) x joins the level of its NEW count
    top = max(top, f)                  # 3) one cursor tracks the highest non-empty level
pop_most():
    x = levels[top].pop()              # newest value that reached the top count
    freq[x] -= 1
    if levels[top] is empty: top -= 1  # the level below is non-empty: x itself is on it
```

@fig-ds-a3 shows the levels this produces; the cell below builds them and checks the cursor.

```{python}
a3_freq = defaultdict(int)
a3_levels = defaultdict(list)
a3_top = 0
for x in [4, 4, 2, 4, 2]:
    a3_freq[x] += 1
    f = a3_freq[x]
    a3_levels[f].append(x)
    a3_top = max(a3_top, f)
assert a3_top == 3 and a3_levels[3] == [4]          # 4 is the only value at count 3
assert a3_levels[2] == [4, 2] and a3_levels[1] == [4, 2]
# pop the top level; it empties, so the cursor drops by exactly one
assert a3_levels[3].pop() == 4
a3_freq[4] -= 1
assert not a3_levels[3]
a3_top -= 1
assert a3_top == 2 and a3_levels[2][-1] == 2        # 2 was the most recent to reach count 2
```

```cpp
// count -> stack of values that reached it, plus an integer cursor for the top level
unordered_map<int, int> freq;               // value -> count
unordered_map<int, vector<int>> levels;     // count -> values that reached it, in order
int topLevel = 0;
void bump(int x) {
    topLevel = max(topLevel, ++freq[x]);
    levels[freq[x]].push_back(x);
}
int popMost() {
    int x = levels[topLevel].back(); levels[topLevel].pop_back(); --freq[x];
    if (levels[topLevel].empty()) --topLevel;
    return x;
}
```

::: {#fig-ds-a3}

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]
a3_fig_levels = defaultdict(list)
a3_fig_freq = Counter()
for x in [4, 4, 2, 4, 2]:
    a3_fig_freq[x] += 1
    a3_fig_levels[a3_fig_freq[x]].append(str(x))
a3_rows = [a3_fig_levels[f] for f in (1, 2, 3)]
assert a3_rows == [["4", "2"], ["4", "2"], ["4"]]


def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, a3_rows, row_labels=["count 1", "count 2", "count 3  (top)"],
           colors={(2, 0): "amber", (1, 1): "cyan"}, cell_w=1.0)
V.show(draw)
```
